analysis.one_liner: Keeps federal agency headquarters and jobs in the Washington area unless Congress approves a move.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require congressional approval before federal agencies could move their headquarters or DC-area jobs out of the Washington region, was referred to committee and has not moved.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lock in the status quo for federal agencies: any headquarters or any employee job based in the Washington, DC area would have to stay there unless Congress itself passes a law approving the move. The stated purpose is to prevent a president or agency head from unilaterally relocating offices and jobs, a step that can push career civil servants to quit or move. It would shift relocation decisions from the executive branch to Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Career federal employees whose jobs are in the Washington region, who could not be required to move or uproot their lives by an agency relocation without Congress acting, and the DC-area economy that depends on federal offices and payrolls.

how_it_helps.text: Any federal employee position with a duty station in the National Capital region would have to remain there unless legislation approving the relocation is enacted into law [S2].
Federal agency headquarters located in the National Capital region would likewise stay put without a new law approving the move [S2].
The bill's stated purpose is to protect federal agencies and employees from political interference, meaning politically driven relocations that displace the workforce [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Any administration or agency leadership that wants the flexibility to relocate headquarters or DC-area jobs to other parts of the country without a congressional vote; the bill also forecloses savings that could come from moving offices to lower-cost areas.

drawbacks.text: Mandating congressional approval for every relocation would take away flexibility to place offices where the work is done, nearer the people or infrastructure an agency serves, which is a common argument for moving federal jobs out of the DC region [S2].
Relocations can move jobs to communities with lower costs and more affordable housing; requiring an act of Congress for each one would make such moves far harder to accomplish [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects DC-area federal workers from politically driven relocations, but it does so by taking relocation decisions away from agencies entirely and requiring an act of Congress for each move. That is a strong shield for one region and one workforce, and a real loss of flexibility for agencies that might serve the country better with offices elsewhere. The cost of the protection falls on everyone outside the DC region who might benefit from federal jobs moving their way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, and nothing has happened since; Congress is still in session, so it is not dead yet.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the bill in the House on March 3, 2025 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform the same day [S1].
No further action has been recorded since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has been materially affected yet: the bill has not advanced and the current rules, under which the executive branch can relocate agencies on its own, remain in place. An administration that wants to relocate DC-area jobs is better off with the bill stalled.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Whoever wants to relocate federal jobs

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.role: Non-voting Delegate for DC; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has taken no further recorded action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill has drawn no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan lineup exists yet; its sponsor is a Democrat.

industries.industry: DC-area federal workforce and government office economy
industries.note: The bill locks in the jobs, payrolls, and office occupancy that federal headquarters and DC-area duty stations bring to the Washington region. For the workers themselves it means protection from forced moves; for the region's office landlords and service economy it means steady demand.

Communities outside the capital region have pushed to host relocated federal offices for the jobs they bring; requiring a new law for each move would make that far harder. Workers outside DC who might take those jobs are the same people this blocks.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action two years into the session, and a sponsor who cannot vote on the floor, the bill is very unlikely to advance; it will most likely expire in committee at the end of this Congress unless support appears.
